blocks.text: Guggenheim 2026: Allison Grant
© Allison Grant, left: Elvira Holding Saint Andrew’s Cross, right: Isa Holding Camphor Weed

Over the next few months, we are featuring the work of many of the 2026 Guggenheim Fellows as a way to celebrate their achievements and understand legacies and projects that have brought them this tremendous recognition.

The Board of Trustees of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation announced their appointment of the 101st class of Guggenheim Fellows, including 223 distinguished individuals working across 55 disciplines. Chosen through a rigorous application and peer review process from a pool of nearly 5,000 applicants, the Class of 2026 Guggenheim Fellows was tapped based on both prior career achievement and exceptional promise. As established in 1925 by founder Senator Simon Guggenheim, each Fellow receives a monetary stipend to pursue independent work at the highest level under “the freest possible conditions.”

“Our new class of Guggenheim Fellows is representative of the world’s best thinkers, innovators, and creators in art, science, and scholarship,” said Edward Hirsch, award-winning poet and President of the Guggenheim Foundation. “As the Foundation enters its second century and looks to the future, I feel confident that this new class of 223 individuals will do bold and inspiring work, undaunted by the challenges ahead. We are honored to support their visionary contributions.”
Allison Grant is an artist and Associate Professor of Photography at The University of Alabama.
Her artworks have been widely exhibited and are held in collections at institutions including the

Bainbridge Island Museum of Art, Birmingham Museum of Art, High Museum of Art, and the Museum of Contemporary Photography. Her work has been published in The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal. She is a 2026 Guggenheim Fellow and was named to the Silver Eye Center for Photography’s 2022 Silver List, among other honors. She lives and works in Tuscaloosa, Alabama.
Find her on Instagram @allie__grant

© Allison Grant, Installation and artist book in the exhibition We Handed Them to Others, As All Good Gardeners Do, Spring Grove Art Gallery at The University of Alabama, Huntsville, Installation Photo by Makalya Miller (4812 Photography)

I was moved when I saw work from your earlier project at the Dangerous Landscapes exhibit at Alabama Contemporary Art Center. Knowing the potential impact of your work during this particular time in history, I was excited to read that you had been awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship and were working on a new project. What does receiving a fellowship mean to you at this stage of your career?

Thanks Karen, I remember talking with you about Dangerous Landscapes . That exhibit was one of the first times I experimented with an installation that invites audience participation. My new work that was awarded a Guggenheim builds on that interest.

But to answer your question, winning a Guggenheim has given me a year to dedicate myself to my art practice full time, which is an incredible gift. In addition to being an artist, I’m also an educator, parent, and sometimes I curate. I love it all, but it’s a lot to manage. As my career has expanded, each of these parts of my life has required more and more attention, and I am always scraping together time and trying to invest further. It can be especially challenging because I make long-term bodies of work that are deeply researched and require a lot of focused consideration. I feel unbelievably fortunate to receive the funds and support to dedicate myself to making new work, and I’m so excited to see what this opportunity makes possible.
© Allison Grant, Top: Lorelei Holding Beebalm, bottom: Kelly and Gwen Holding Tansy
© Allison Grant, Top: Lorelei Holding Beebalm, bottom: Kelly and Gwen Holding Tansy
Did the fellowship validate something you already knew about your work, or did it change how you see your practice?

I have spent the last ten years living and working in Tuscaloosa, Alabama. It is a place with a lot of political and social tension, but also one that is often stereotyped and flattened by the national news media and ignored by the contemporary art world. In my work and life, I’ve become interested in broadening the ways the Deep South is seen and known in relation to national and international issues, and forging possibilities for coalitions and understanding with people from other regions. The Guggenheim is a kind of affirmation of the work I’ve done in community, and to me it also draws attention to a place and its people, and not just me as an artist. What the fellowship validated for me is the power of working alongside others through a practice that is braided with the wisdom, strength, and openness of my community, and especially people I’ve come to know in the American South.

The award felt extra gratifying because Jeremiah Ariaz and Harlan Bozeman , who both live in the Deep South, and Chris Aluka Berry , who works in Appalachia, were in the same cohort as me. Seeing them awarded felt like a further recognition that the stories coming out of overlooked regions of America are finding a larger place in contemporary art.
© Allison Grant, Seif Holding Hellebore
Tell us about your current project.

It’s called Holding Together . For the past two years, I’ve been photographing people in Alabama and other parts of the US while they hold plants that have been historically used for contraception, abortion, or infertility treatment.

The 2022 Dobbs decision made reproductive healthcare much more difficult to access, especially in the Deep South. I wanted to make a community portrait of people contending with this new legal landscape. I started researching plants that people used to try to manage fertility before modern medical treatments were available. Many of the plants have interesting histories: tansy and hellebore were documented as abortifacients in medieval monastic medical records [1] ; dogfennel is listed in the Native American Ethnobotany Database as an Indigenous abortifacient [1] ; cotton was used by enslaved Black women to induce abortion using knowledge brought from parts of Africa where cotton grows wild [2] ; and Queen Anne’s Lace has been used in various cultural contexts as an emergency contraceptive, including in Appalachian communities where people have sometimes been cut off from healthcare, physically and financially. [3]

Other folk remedies exist, too, but they are almost all ineffective or toxic, and should not be used. I wanted to work with my community to honor the long history of people using these plants, while also refusing to accept a world where they become someone’s only option today. As I photographed, subjects often shared stories of their experiences with reproductive healthcare and their motivations for participating. I started recording these stories and including transcriptions of them in installations as a way of embedding the present into longer histories.

When we were talking earlier about my exhibition at Alabama Contemporary, I mentioned my interest in involving visitors as participants. A few months ago, I showed two images from Holding Together at the Sarah Moody Art Gallery at The University of Alabama. Beneath the photographs were postcards with the same images that visitors could take and mail. Mail order abortion pills have been a critical lifeline for many people in states with bans, and the postcards are a way for viewers to participate in the project by symbolically mailing abortifacients. It’s one way I’m thinking about how I might extend this work beyond the gallery.
[1] John M. Riddle, Eve’s Herbs: A History of Contraception and Abortion in the West (Harvard University Press, 1997).
[1] Daniel E. Moerman, “Dogfennel,” Native American Ethnobotany, University of Michigan, Dearborn, accessed September 3, 2026, http://naeb.brit.org/uses/9140/.
[2] Dorothy Roberts, Killing the Black Body: Race, Reproduction, and the Meaning of Liberty (Pantheon Books, 1997).
[3] Gabrielle Claire Jansen and Hans Wohlmuth, “Carrot Seed for Contraception: A Review,” Australian Journal of Herbal Medicine 26, no. 1 (2014): 10–17.
© Allison Grant, T. and Maziyar Holding Rue
You mentioned your hope to forge possibilities for coalitions and understanding. Would you elaborate?
Yes, let me share a story that will help explain.

When the Dobbs decision was announced, I was visiting Chicago and while I was in town I attended a Women in the Arts luncheon. Many people at the event were processing the upsetting news we’d all heard that morning. I went to graduate school in Chicago, and I had a conversation with a few people from that community whom I deeply respect. They were angry because they believed that Southerners were to blame for a ruling that had made women and people with uteruses in Chicago unsafe.

In my opinion, that is a skewed understanding. There are people in the Deep South who fight for reproductive justice and work under some of the most difficult circumstances in the country. Their work is often unseen in other regions where people sometimes have a limited understanding of what is happening here. One motivation for this project is to push against bias against this region because it is not accurate. 48% of Alabamians believe abortion should be legal in most or all cases. [1]

I want to make art that brings visibility and support to the many people living in the Deep South who are fighting for the same things as the women I was talking with in Chicago on that day. I don’t share this story to humiliate or scold anyone. I want to work together, and one hope I have is that visibility will make space for coalitions and shared advocacy that is sometimes hindered by stereotypes about the South.

[1] Public Religion Research Institute, “Mapping Abortion Views Across the 50 States: Insights from PRRI’s2025 American Values Atlas,” April 23, 2026, https://prri.org/research/mapping-abortion-views-across-the-50-states-insights-from-prris-2025-american-values-atlas/ .

© Allison Grant, Installation and artist book in the exhibition We Handed Them to Others, As All Good Gardeners Do, Spring Grove Art Gallery at The University of Alabama, Huntsville, Installation Photo by Makalya Miller (4812 Photography)
How will you use the freedom The Guggenheim Fellowship provides?

I am working to expand the geographic reach and scope of Holding Together . Most of the photographs and interviews in the project have come from a network of contacts and reproductive healthcare advocacy organizations in Alabama. I want to incorporate a more robust understanding of how reproductive experiences differ across places, and I want that expansion to grow out of meaningful relationships that I build with people I meet and interact with in person. The fellowship will allow me to travel and follow what develops.

As I travel, I’d like to visit libraries and archives with collections that hold books, zines, and other parts of the material history of the transmission of reproductive medical knowledge. I’ve photographed older women who’ve described zines that circulated pre-internet with instructions on using herbal contraceptives and abortifacients. I’ve also found examples housed in academic libraries alongside books and archival materials that describe historic methods and experiences. Before contemporary pharmaceutical systems, botanical illustrations, and eventually photographic technologies, were essential tools for identifying plants and communicating knowledge about their medicinal uses.

These materials already play a role in my thinking. My photographs are printed on matte paper and they kind of look like a drawing. This is intentional—I am trying to nod to the history of botanical illustration and blur the line between drawing and photography, and between two-dimensional representation and photographic depth. As I continue to explore, I’m curious to see if more elements of research might inform or even enter my work.
I am also using this time to create a book. I think this project is perfectly suited to the intimacy and slowness a book can offer, and I’m excited by the drafts I’ve put together so far.
© Allison Grant, Bet Holding Hellebore

Thank you for sharing some of the pages from your upcoming book with us today. Your last book, Within The Bittersweet , was about raising your children amid concerns of climate change and pollution. It is a gorgeous book that merges themes of beauty and grief. Are there commonalities between that project and Holding Together?
Yes, many. Both projects are rooted in questions about how we care for ourselves and others while contending with difficult realities of our time.

They are also both filled with grief and awe at the many things women have survived. I don’t think people talk about the constant grief and complexity inside of pregnancy, motherhood or living in a body capable of reproduction nearly as much as it’s felt. I feel it is powerful to put that on display. Having public facing art exhibitions is very important to me because it creates a way for others to consider stories usually kept in private life.
© Allison Grant, Allison Holding Hellebore
© Allison Grant, SJW Holding Leatherleaf Mahonia, Constantine Holding Epazote and Wormwood
How has Holding Together impacted you as a mother, a woman, an educator, and an artist?

People have died in my community while waiting for an emergency D&C that doctors can’t give. Both this project and Within the Bittersweet have forced me to contend with the limits of my ability to protect myself and the people I love. I feel like every story I’ve recorded for Holding Together could have been me if I were born into different circumstances or with different anatomy, and I worry my daughters could live versions of those stories too. We are so lucky to live in a time when medical advances make high-quality care possible, but if we do not have access, our children and communities will not be safe. How does one show up in a world where that is true? Things will never change for the better if no one is willing to look it in the face, so that’s what I try to do with as much kindness and humility as I can.
© Allison Grant, Sydney Holding Cotton
© Allison Grant, Hallie Holding Queen Anne’s Lace, Sarah and Milo Holding Queen Anne’s Lace

As I read the words accompanying your photographs, I hear both vulnerability and courage in the sharing of these stories. Will you tell us a bit about creating an atmosphere of trust while working on this project? Also, have any of the people you have photographed and interviewed shared the impact of their participation in this project on their own lives?

Yes. It is important to me to avoid harming participants or anyone who is discussed in a story. I have interviewed immigrants and people who could face legal consequences, workplace backlash, or community ostracization for talking openly about these issues. Before I interview someone, I let them know that I won’t share their identity. After we finish, I transcribe what was said, clean it up, and take anything too specific out in consultation with the subject. Once they’ve signed off, I let them know where I’ll be publishing it and I tell them they can withdraw from the project at any time. I came up with this process with help from several community historians at The University of Alabama.

The photographs are titled with the first names of the subjects unless they ask me to withhold their identity. Names can signal background, identity, and ethnicity, and the pictures aren’t as specific, so my approach is a little different there.

A lot of the people I’ve included in my work find the process of participating cathartic. Reproductive healthcare has a profound impact on people’s lives. Sharing helps the narrator and the reader know they are not alone. Every time I photograph or interview someone, I feel a million times closer to them when we finish, and I think that’s mutual. It’s the best part of making the work.

Many of the stories I’m told end with a sense of healing or personal resolution. In difficult experiences, I think individuals need that kind of closure. But for the project, I often ask subjects if I can take those end parts out. On a societal level, their experiences echo things that are still happening. I think taking the resolution out makes the stories feel more true to the larger ideas in the project, and subjects usually agree.
© Allison Grant, Grace Holding Tansy
© Allison Grant, top: Grace Holding Tansy, bottom: Arielle Holding Juniper What has sustained your practice over the years?

Friendships and community, first and foremost. There are people who have been the first eyes and ears on my work for most of my adult life. I’ve found a kind of mutual trust in these relationships, and we’ve come to see each other’s perspectives in ways that are very deep and powerful.

Grants have also sustained my practice. The generous donors and organizations who offer financial support, like the Guggenheim, are a lifeline. We’ve been watching the federal government gut funding, and there is an implicit pressure that many institutions are weighing when they consider showing politically charged artwork. I’ve been really lucky to work with several organizations and institutions that are willing to hold space for viewpoints that are under attack. Not every museum or institution will do it, and it’s empowering to watch an organization put their values on the line alongside an artist instead of shrinking back.
© Allison Grant, Shakiba Holding Yarrow, Claire Holding Queen Anne’s Lace
© Allison Grant, Alesha Holding Queen Anne’s Lace
Thank you, Allison. In closing, what advice would you give to photographers for going through the process of applying for a fellowship?

Find a community and engage generously. Art is built through reciprocity and shared support, and your application will be stronger if you are submitting something that’s received feedback from people you trust.

I also think it’s important to consider what you have to gain if you don’t win. I applied three times. I learned so much about myself and my work every time. I had support readers who told me how strong my applications were and made me feel like I was moving my practice forward, even when I wasn’t awarded. That’s the way I try to look at all of the work that I do. Applying can affirm a belief in the value of my work that doesn’t have to be shredded every time I get a rejection.
